strengths: The paper targets a genuinely under-explored problem — interpretable facial forgery localization — and the motivation that binary masks alone cannot explain forgery predictions is well argued and timely given the rise of diffusion-based face manipulation.

The MMTT dataset is a substantial resource contribution: 128,303 image–mask–text triplets built from CelebA-HQ and FFHQ, covering three manipulation paradigms (GAN-based face swapping, transformer-based and diffusion-based inpainting), with a documented human annotation pipeline including time constraints, length constraints, and a screening step for false-positive regions.

The dataset statistics are reported in reasonable detail (manipulation type distribution, modified-part frequencies, caption length distributions), and a comparison table against existing forgery datasets clearly positions MMTT's novelty in adding textual annotations.

The model design (Forgery Prompter Network feeding region prompts into an InstructBLIP-based pipeline with a SAM-style mask decoder) is a sensible integration, and the two-stage training and losses are described concretely enough to be implementable.
The authors commit to releasing the dataset, code, and pretrained checkpoints, which would materially aid reproducibility.

The ablation (Table 3) is informative: the large CIDEr gap between FPN-GT (48.1) and predicted FPN (21.5) honestly exposes the region-prediction bottleneck, and Table 4 isolates the contributions of the CoordConv/conv branch and BCE+Dice loss.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to the authors' own dataset with an 8:1:1 split; there is no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution evaluation (e.g., real-world or unseen manipulation methods), so generalization claims are unsupported — a major concern for a forgery-detection resource whose practical value depends on generalization.

The headline claim of 'superior performance' is overstated: the model loses to SCA on IoU (70.81 vs 72.87), to InstructBLIP on ROUGE-L, and gains over InstructBLIP are marginal (CIDEr 21.5 vs 20.9, BLEU-1 31.1 vs 30.6). The claim of 'better average performance across multiple criteria' is an ad hoc aggregate rather than a principled comparison.

Captioning metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, METEOR) are weak proxies for explanation quality; there is no human evaluation of the generated interpretations (fluency, factual correctness about the manipulated regions), which is essential given the paper's interpretability focus. Factual consistency between generated text and the ground-truth mask is never quantified.

Annotation quality control is thin for a dataset intended as the primary benchmark: a 1-minute minimum per image and 'simple screening' of false positives are weak guarantees; no inter-annotator agreement, no verification pass on a held-out sample, and the reported throughput (~20 images/hour across 30 annotators) raises doubt about annotation depth. The known-label issue is also a concern: annotators see the ground-truth mask and the original image, so captions may encode manipulation-method artifacts rather than visually detectable cues.

It is unclear how the baselines (SCA, LISA-7B, Osprey, InstructBLIP) were adapted to this task (fine-tuning protocol, prompts, training budget), making the comparison potentially unfair and hard to reproduce.

There are numerous citation errors undermining scholarly rigor: [42] is cited for CelebAMask-HQ but the reference is CelebV-HQ (a different paper); [1] is cited for E4S but is a GAN industry review; references [2] and [7] are duplicate ViT entries. Terminology is also inconsistent ('Tramper' vs 'Tampering' in the dataset name, 'ForgerTalker' vs 'ForgeryTalker'), and the text contains frequent typos ('Quatitative', 'develope', 'resutls', 'interpreatation').

The FPN's PLM of only 41% means the deployed system operates far from the ideal (FPN-GT) regime, and the paper offers no analysis of error modes (e.g., whether failures correlate with subtle manipulations the paper argues are most important).
Privacy/ethics considerations are addressed only implicitly; face images from CelebA-HQ/FFHQ plus forgery annotations warrant explicit discussion of consent, dual-use, and intended-use restrictions.

Relevance to the ACL/NLP community is partial: the core contribution is a vision-centric dataset and segmentation-plus-captioning model; the NLP component (instruction-tuned MLLM explanation generation) is standard and the language side is evaluated only with n-gram metrics.

strengths: The problem of interpretable forgery localization (predicting both manipulation masks and textual explanations) is a reasonable and timely extension of deepfake detection, and the paper is positioned as an early study of this task.

The scale of the data collection effort is substantial: ~128K image-text-mask triplets built from CelebA-HQ and FFHQ using three manipulation families (GAN face swapping, transformer inpainting, diffusion inpainting), with a documented annotation pipeline, guidelines, and a two-phase annotation schedule.

The proposed ForgeryTalker architecture (Forgery Prompter Network + SAM-style mask decoder on top of InstructBLIP) is described at a level of detail (losses, training schedule, hyperparameters) that is mostly sufficient to understand the method.

Ablations (w/ FPN-GT, w/o FPN, loss and discount-factor variants for the prompter) are sensible and help isolate the contribution of the FPN, showing that accurate region prompts substantially improve caption quality (CIDEr 48.1 vs 21.5).
The authors commit to releasing the dataset, code, and checkpoints, which would support reproducibility if fulfilled.
weaknesses: Weak evidence of improvement over the baseline: InstructBLIP alone already achieves CIDEr 20.9 vs. ForgeryTalker's 21.5, with the FPN yielding only a ~0.6 CIDEr gain and mixed localization results (lower recall than InstructBLIP, lower IoU than SCA). The 'superior performance' claim is not convincingly supported; absolute caption quality is also very low (CIDEr ~21, BLEU-4 ~5.9), and no human evaluation of explanation quality is provided despite interpretability being the paper's central motivation.

All experiments are train/test on the authors' own synthetic dataset. There is no cross-dataset evaluation, no test on real or unseen manipulation methods, and no evidence the models generalize beyond the specific generation pipelines used to build MMTT. Given the paper's framing around modern forgery threats, this is a significant gap.

Annotation quality control is thin: the stated QC consists of a one-minute minimum per image and a 'simple screening' that removes labels on non-manipulated regions. No inter-annotator agreement, no spot-check accuracy rates, no analysis of caption factual consistency, and unclear details on annotator recruitment/compensation/conditions. Quality claims ('high-quality, reliable labels') are asserted rather than measured.

Circularity concern: annotators are shown the ground-truth manipulation mask while writing descriptions, and the FPN's 21-way region labels are extracted from those same annotations. The evaluation thus partly measures whether the model recovers the annotation distribution induced by the mask, not whether explanations reflect genuine forensic evidence.

Numerous errors undermine confidence: the dataset name oscillates among 'Tramper Tracing,' 'Tampering Tracing,' and 'Trampering'; the model is called both 'ForgeryTalker' and 'ForgerTalker'; 'Quatitative,' 'interpreatation,' 'resutls,' 'unmodifed,' 'develope' appear in the text. Citation errors include [1] (a GAN-applications review) cited for the E4S face-swapping model, and [42] (CelebV-HQ) cited as CelebAMask-HQ. Table 3's 'w/o FPN' row is identical to the InstructBLIP row in Table 2, suggesting the 'ablation' is simply the untuned baseline.

Baselines are not clearly described as fine-tuned on MMTT under matched conditions, making cross-model comparisons (e.g., SCA's SAM-based IoU advantage being attributed to architecture rather than adaptation) hard to interpret.

No ethics statement despite a dataset of manipulated real-face images derived from CelebA-HQ and FFHQ, with no discussion of consent, misuse potential, or safeguards for releasing a large deepfake-generation corpus; this falls short of ACL expectations.

Formatting follows a CVPR-style template rather than ACL, and the related work section is superficial with some mischaracterized citations; relevance and presentation are below the bar for ACL's main track.

Reproducibility is currently promised but not demonstrated: no released data/code at review time, and the FPN's own performance (PLM only 41%) is acknowledged as weak, leaving the pipeline's key component under-validated.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely relevant and underexplored task: interpretable face forgery localization, combining pixel-level masks with textual explanations, which is timely given the rise of diffusion-based manipulation.

The MMTT dataset is substantial in scale (128,303 image-text-mask triplets) and built with a documented, multi-stage human annotation pipeline, including quality-control constraints (minimum observation time, length limits, false-positive screening) and a two-phase refinement process.

The dataset construction protocol is described in enough detail (source corpora, three manipulation methods with generation formulas, region-sampling procedures, annotation instructions) that the resource could plausibly be reproduced by others, and the authors commit to releasing data, code, and checkpoints.
Table 1 provides a useful comparison of MMTT against existing forgery benchmarks, clearly delineating the gap MMTT fills (text annotations paired with masks).

The ablation includes an informative upper-bound variant (FPN-GT, CIDEr 48.1) demonstrating the headroom if region prompts were accurate, and a component ablation (Table 4) on the discount factor and loss design.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to the authors' own MMTT test split. There is no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution evaluation, and it is not specified whether the baselines (SCA, LISA-7B, Osprey, InstructBLIP) were fine-tuned on MMTT or evaluated zero-shot; this ambiguity makes the comparison in Table 2 difficult to interpret and the 'superior performance' claim weakly supported.

The main architectural contribution (FPN) is undermined by the paper's own results: PLM is only 41%, and removing FPN changes CIDEr from 21.5 to 20.9 (the 'w/o FPN' row is numerically identical to InstructBLIP in Table 2, suggesting it is simply the untuned baseline). The gap between w/ FPN (21.5) and w/ FPN-GT (48.1) is presented as motivation, but the actual FPN closes almost none of it, so the headline method provides marginal benefit.

Results are mixed rather than superior: ForgeryTalker trails SCA in IoU (70.81 vs 72.87) and InstructBLIP in ROUGE-L (24.3 vs 24.8), and absolute captioning scores (CIDEr 21.5, BLEU-4 5.9) are very low. No human evaluation of explanation quality is provided, so whether the generated interpretations are actually useful/faithful is unverified.

A structural tension in the annotation design: annotators see the original image and the ground-truth mask, but are told not to reference the original. This risks descriptions that rationalize the mask (post-hoc) rather than describe visually detectable artifacts, which would inflate apparent alignment between text and masks. No inter-annotator agreement, no measure of whether described artifacts are genuinely visible in the forged image alone, and the 'simple screening' (removing labels for non-manipulated regions) is too weak to validate text faithfulness.

Significant writing and consistency problems undermine confidence: the dataset name shifts among 'Tramper Tracing,' 'Tampering Tracing,' and 'Tamper Tracing'; typos throughout ('Quatitative,' 'interpreatation,' 'resutls,' 'unmodifed,' 'articuture,' 'ForgerTalker'); the Related Work section abruptly claims 'Our ViT-based classifier bridges this gap' in a passage that does not match the proposed model; and dataset statistics are internally inconsistent (Eye region counts of 66,403 vs 108,750; Eyebrow 83,594 vs 83,606).

The claim of an 'unexplored problem' is overstated; explanation-oriented and multimodal deepfake analysis exists in prior work, and the related-work discussion does not adequately engage the closest precedents.

Missing ethical detail for an ACL-relevant human-subjects resource: no information on annotator demographics, compensation, consent, or data protection; the use of CelebA-HQ/FFHQ face images to create deepfakes also raises licensing/consent and dual-use concerns that are not addressed beyond a general threat framing.

Reproducibility gaps: the 21-class region label space is only loosely defined (how the 21 semantics map to CelebAMask-HQ components and Dlib segments is unclear), and promised public release is stated but not yet verifiable.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new task (Forgery Attribution Report Generation) combining forgery localization and natural language explanation, which is well-motivated and relevant to interpretable multimodal NLP and to the ACL community's interest in multimodal misinformation.

MMTT is a substantial resource: 152,217 image–mask–text triplets built from a clearly documented, programmatic forgery process (process-derived masks avoid registration error) plus a structured human annotation pipeline with quality controls (guidelines, minimum observation time, automatic flagging of out-of-mask descriptions).

The experimental section is broad: comparisons against zero-shot LVLMs and fine-tuned specialists, ablations for the FPN and pretraining stage, oracle (FPN-GT) upper bounds, leave-one-manipulation-type-out analysis, and zero-shot transfer to DQ_F++ and SynthScars.

The paper includes thorough ethics (dual-use risk, DUA-restricted release, exclusion of minors) and reproducibility statements, plus detailed appendices with training/evaluation protocols, hyperparameters, and loss formulations, which supports reproducibility.

The proposed ForgeryTalker baseline is coherent and its design choices (shared encoder, dual decoders, region-prompting FPN) are clearly motivated and analyzed; ablations show each component contributes.
weaknesses: Evaluation of the textual explanations relies exclusively on n-gram metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/ROUGE) against single references. There is no human evaluation of explanation factuality, grounding, or usefulness, which is the crux of the claimed contribution. Since a report can score well while asserting hallucinated artifacts, the central claim that models generate trustworthy 'evidence' is only weakly supported.

Ground-truth annotation quality control is comparatively thin: no inter-annotator agreement statistics, no verification that in-mask descriptions correspond to actual artifacts (annotators could describe plausible-looking but non-existent inconsistencies), and no audit of description–mask consistency beyond out-of-mask flagging.

The 'why' supervision is tied to artifacts of specific generative models (E4S, StyleCLIP/HFGI, MAT, SDXL). There is a risk that models exploit generation-specific shortcuts rather than general forensics evidence; the SynthScars zero-shot results (CIDEr 2.2, very low absolute scores) suggest limited stylistic/generalization transfer, and the paper downplays this.
The baseline is architecturally incremental (InstructBLIP + SAM two-way decoder + a multi-label prompter with coord-conv), so the methodological novelty beyond the dataset is limited.

Several citation and writing problems reduce polish: the E4S citation appears to point to an unrelated survey, the U-Net/DeepLab claim cites the focal-loss paper, the ViT reference is malformed ('Dosovitskiy Alexey. 2020.'), and repeated 'i.e.,,' typos appear throughout.

The abstract claims 'the first large-scale dataset' with textual explanations; the related-work discussion of FakeShield (which also produces explanations) makes the differentiation mostly about domain and human annotation, and this distinction could be argued more carefully.
No released artifacts at review time (code/data/checkpoints are only promised), so reproducibility currently rests on the documentation rather than on verifiable releases.
Some inconsistencies (e.g., full-set ablation numbers in Table 9 differ from the main results in Table 2, without explanation) raise questions about experiment bookkeeping.

strengths: The proposed task—joint forgery localization and natural-language explanation—is practically motivated, and moving from binary 'verdicts' to interpretable 'evidence' is a relevant direction for multimodal forensics and connects to NLP interests in grounded explanation generation.

MMTT is a large-scale resource (152,217 triplets) combining process-derived masks with human-authored descriptions, and the annotation pipeline (guidelines, minimum observation time, false-positive flagging, region-constrained descriptions) is described at a level of detail that supports future replication of the annotation process.

The experimental section is fairly comprehensive: baselines span zero-shot LVLMs, specialist localization models, and fine-tuned captioning models; ablations cover the FPN, the pretraining stage, loss components, and leave-one-type-out data composition; supplementary results extend to DQ_F++, SynthScars, and a state-of-the-art comparison.

The paper includes appropriate ethics (dual-use risk discussion, DUA-based release, screening for minors), reproducibility commitments, and an LLM usage statement, and implementation details (GPU, training schedule, hyperparameters, splits) are reported.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim of being 'the first' to provide textual explanations alongside forgery masks is overstated. The paper itself evaluates on DQ_F++ (Zhang et al., 2024b), a deepfake benchmark with natural-language rationales, yet Table 1 omits it from the dataset comparison; Legion (cited in references as 'Learning to ground and explain for synthetic image detection') and FakeShield address closely related grounding+explanation tasks but are never properly positioned against. The related-work treatment of the closest competitors is inadequate.

Absolute text-generation quality is weak and unexamined: CIDEr of 59.3 and BLEU-4 of 12.5 on the paper's own dataset are low, and the corpus statistics (dominance of formulaic phrases like 'not clear', 'blurry', 'indistinct' visible in the word cloud and examples) suggest highly templated annotations. There is no human evaluation of explanation usefulness, fluency, or faithfulness—yet 'explainability for human reviewers' is the core motivating claim.

Annotation reliability is under-evidenced. The paper reports no inter-annotator agreement, no per-sample annotator counts, and no audit results for the automatic false-positive flagging. Since annotators are instructed to describe artifacts only within the process-derived mask, there is a real risk of forced/contrived descriptions (describing normal variation as 'inconsistencies'), which would undermine the 'why' supervision; this is never validated.

Internal inconsistencies raise soundness concerns: the 'Full Set' results in the leave-one-type-out ablation (IoU 71.00, CIDEr 56.9) do not match the main results (IoU 73.67, CIDEr 59.3) with no explanation; several Table 2 rows appear misaligned (e.g., FFAA and FakeShield BLEU-3/BLEU-4/ROUGE-L values violate metric monotonicity); and DQ_F++ zero-shot in Table 3 contradicts the SynthScars setup where all models are explicitly fine-tuned on MMTT—clarity on transfer settings is needed.

The headline comparison is somewhat apples-to-oranges: zero-shot LVLMs (with near-zero CIDEr) are contrasted against a model fine-tuned on in-domain data, making the 'order of magnitude' improvement unsurprising; the more informative comparisons (fine-tuned InstructBLIP, LISA) show narrower gaps, and the oracle FPN-GT ablation (CIDEr 95.1 vs. 59.3) reveals that the model's performance is heavily bottlenecked by its own prompt module.

Reproducibility currently rests on promises: code, data, and checkpoints 'will be released,' and the dataset is gated behind a Data Usage Agreement; additionally, the ethical section states the generation pipelines will not be disclosed, which conflicts with the reproducibility statement and would prevent full reconstruction of the dataset.

Writing and presentation issues recur throughout (e.g., 'i.e.,,' typos, duplicated figure content in Figure 2, dense equations restating standard losses), and the framing is largely vision/forensics-oriented with limited linguistic analysis of the annotation corpus, weakening the CL-specific contribution beyond the existence of text annotations.

strengths: The paper introduces a clearly motivated new task—Forgery Attribution Report Generation—that combines pixel-level forgery localization with natural language explanation, going beyond binary classification/mask-only forensics and connecting the multimodal forensics and vision-language communities.

MMTT is a large-scale (152,217 samples) benchmark whose ground-truth masks are programmatically derived from the editing process (ensuring alignment) and whose textual explanations are human-authored, which is a unique feature compared to prior forgery datasets (Table 1).

The annotation pipeline is described in reasonable detail (guidelines, region-constrained descriptions, length limits, automated flagging of out-of-mask references), and dataset statistics (manipulation-type distribution, modified facial parts, caption length) are analyzed.

The baseline (ForgeryTalker) is a sensible, well-specified architecture (InstructBLIP-style encoder + Q-Former, SAM-based mask decoder, Forgery Prompter Network) with a clearly defined two-stage training procedure and explicit loss formulations.

The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive: comparisons against fine-tuned specialist models and zero-shot LVLMs, zero-shot generalization tests on DQ_F++ and SynthScars, and multiple ablations (FPN, pretraining stage, loss components, leave-one-manipulation-type-out) that provide insight into which data types drive localization vs. generation performance.
The paper includes ethics (dual-use mitigation, DUA-gated release, exclusion of minors), reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements, and commits to releasing code, data, and checkpoints.
weaknesses: Evaluation of the explanation component relies entirely on n-gram metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/ROUGE). For a paper whose central contribution is human-interpretable explanation, there is no human evaluation of explanation faithfulness, correctness, or usefulness, and no analysis of whether high CIDEr actually reflects valid forensic evidence. This is the most significant gap between the paper's claims and its evidence.

Annotation reliability is under-supported: no inter-annotator agreement statistics, no number of annotators per sample, no manual audit results are reported. A one-minute minimum observation time and automated out-of-mask flagging are weak proxies for annotation quality, and the QC step ('simple screening') is not formally defined.

The dataset's forgeries are simulated with a fixed, small set of generative models (E4S, StyleCLIP, HFGI, MAT, SDXL), and the human descriptions are anchored to artifacts of these specific pipelines. The zero-shot SynthScars results (CIDEr 2.2) confirm a strong domain/style dependence that limits claims of generalization to real-world forgery explanation.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: zero-shot LVLMs are not fine-tuned while specialists and ForgeryTalker are, so the 'order of magnitude' CIDEr gap over LVLMs (Table 6) largely reflects task-specific training rather than architectural advantage. Table 3's 'zero-shot' DQ_F++ comparison is likewise potentially confounded by caption-style alignment.

The oracle FPN-GT ablation (95.1 vs. 59.3 CIDEr) shows the region-prompt bottleneck is very large, yet the paper offers no analysis of FPN failure modes; there are also minor numerical inconsistencies (e.g., Full Set IoU 71.00/CIDEr 56.90 in Table 9 vs. 73.67/59.3 in Table 2) that are not explained.

The methodological novelty is modest: the architecture is largely a composition of existing components (InstructBLIP, SAM's two-way transformer, coordinate convolution), so the contribution rests mainly on the dataset/task; the paper would benefit from more positioning against concurrent explainable-forgery work (e.g., FakeShield, Legion) rather than brief mentions.

Writing quality issues remain (recurring 'i.e.,,' typos, some citation formatting problems, a missing entry for the cited Kang et al. 2025 SynthScars reference), and several experimental details (loss weights λ, discount factor analysis placement, number of annotation rounds) are scattered or under-specified.
